column2: Your threat hunting team has developed a hypothesis that attackers are using a specific pattern of low-prevalence domains for command and control communication. You want to create a YARA-L rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) that identifies network connections to domains that have been accessed by only one internal asset in your environment. Which enrichment field should you use in your detection rule?
column3: Use the target.domain.reputation_score field to filter for domains with unknown reputation indicating low prevalence.
column4: Query the graph.entity.domain.first_seen_timestamp to identify newly observed domains in the environment.
column5: Create a reference list of known low-prevalence domains and match network events against this static list.
column6: Use the graph.entity.domain.prevalence.rolling_max field set to 1 to identify domains with minimal internal access over a 10-day rolling window.
column8: Google SecOps calculates prevalence statistics that indicate how many unique internal assets have accessed a given domain. The rolling_max field represents the maximum daily prevalence score over the previous 10-day window. A value of 1 indicates the domain was accessed by only one internal asset, which is characteristic of potential C2 infrastructure. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/event-processing/data-enrichment

column2: Your SOC team needs to share a custom Google Security Operations (SecOps) dashboard with another team that operates a separate SecOps instance in a different region. The dashboard contains custom threat visualization charts. What is the correct procedure to accomplish this?
column3: Export the dashboard to a JSON file from your instance and have the other team import the JSON file into their SecOps instance.
column4: Export the dashboard LookML code and provide it to the other team to import into their Looker-based dashboard system.
column5: Configure Workforce Identity Federation to enable cross-instance dashboard access between the two SecOps deployments.
column6: Share the dashboard URL with the other team and grant them viewer access through the dashboard sharing settings.
column8: Google SecOps native dashboards can be exported to JSON files that contain the dashboard layout and filter settings. These JSON files can then be imported into another SecOps instance. This is the supported method for sharing dashboards across instances. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/manage-native-dashboards

column2: Your organization has deployed multiple Event Threat Detection custom modules to detect connections to IOCs from various threat intelligence feeds. During a security incident, you notice that expected findings are not appearing for some IOC matches. You suspect the custom modules may have exceeded a quota limit. What is the default quota limit for custom module findings per parent resource per hour in Event Threat Detection?
column3: 200 findings per parent resource (organization or project) per hour
column4: Unlimited findings with a rate limit of 10 findings per second
column5: 50 findings per custom module per hour
column6: 1000 findings per parent resource (organization or project) per hour
column8: Event Threat Detection custom modules have a quota limit of 200 custom module findings per parent resource per hour. Each finding counts towards either the organization or project quota, depending on which level the source custom module was created. This limit cannot be increased, so organizations with high-volume detection needs should design their custom modules accordingly. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: After configuring a log sink to route security-relevant logs to a Cloud Storage bucket for forensic evidence collection, you discover that the sink was created 3 days after the security incident began. You need to preserve the historical logs from the 3-day gap that were stored in the Cloud Logging _Default bucket. What should you do?
column3: Use the gcloud logging copy command to copy the historical logs from the _Default bucket to the Cloud Storage bucket.
column4: Modify the sink to use a backdated filter to capture logs from the 3-day period before the sink was created.
column5: Export the logs using the Logs Explorer to a local file and manually upload them to the Cloud Storage bucket.
column6: Contact Google Cloud Support to request extraction of the missing logs from Cloud Logging internal archives.
column8: Cloud Logging provides the ability to retroactively copy log entries that are already stored in log buckets to Cloud Storage buckets using the copy logs feature. This allows recovery of logs from the gap period before the sink was configured. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/copy-logs

column2: Your company must comply with SEC Rule 17a-4(f) requirements for retaining security logs for 7 years in an immutable format. You are configuring a Cloud Storage bucket as the destination for security logs routed via Cloud Logging sinks. Which Cloud Storage configuration should you implement to meet the immutability requirement?
column3: Configure the Cloud Storage bucket with Archive storage class and set object retention to 7 years.
column4: Configure a retention policy on the Cloud Storage bucket with a 7-year retention period and lock the policy.
column5: Enable Object Versioning on the Cloud Storage bucket and configure a lifecycle policy to retain versions for 7 years.
column6: Enable customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) and configure Cloud KMS key rotation every 90 days.
column8: Bucket Lock with a locked retention policy ensures objects cannot be deleted or modified until the retention period expires. Once locked, the policy cannot be removed or reduced, meeting WORM (Write Once Read Many) requirements for SEC Rule 17a-4(f), CFTC Rule 1.31(c)-(d), and FINRA Rule 4511(c) compliance. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock

column2: You are establishing a data classification baseline across your organization's Cloud Storage buckets using Sensitive Data Protection. After running discovery scans, you notice that some buckets show a data risk level of 'Unknown.' What is the most likely cause of this status?
column3: The data in the buckets could not be scanned successfully, making it uncertain whether sensitive data exists.
column4: The buckets contain only public data with no access restrictions, resulting in undefined risk classification.
column5: The buckets have been configured with automatic tagging enabled, which sets the data risk level to a placeholder status until reviewed.
column6: The infoTypes specified in the inspection template do not match any data patterns in the buckets.
column8: According to Sensitive Data Protection documentation, an 'Unknown' data risk level indicates that the data couldn't be scanned successfully, leaving uncertainty about whether sensitive data exists. This can occur due to permission issues, unsupported file types, or other scanning failures. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/sensitivity-risk-calculation

column2: You have configured a user-defined log-based metric to count IAM policy changes for security monitoring. When you create an alerting policy based on this metric, you notice false notifications occurring due to gaps in the metric data. You need to reduce false notifications while maintaining effective security alerting. What should you do?
column3: Increase the rolling window value in the alerting policy configuration to at least 10 minutes.
column4: Configure the alerting policy to use metric-absence condition type instead of threshold condition.
column5: Enable auto extraction on the log-based metric to fill in missing data points automatically.
column6: Set the retest window to zero for the most responsive alerting policy configuration.
column8: Log-based metric data can have gaps that result in false notifications. Increasing the rolling window value reduces the risk of false notifications by aggregating data over a longer period, ensuring that multiple log entries matching the filter are counted before the condition is evaluated. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/charts-and-alerts

column2: Your security team needs to monitor for IAM policy changes that grant sensitive roles. You want to be notified immediately when a log entry containing 'SetIamPolicy' with the 'roles/owner' role appears in your audit logs. What is the most appropriate alerting approach?
column3: Configure Event Threat Detection in Security Command Center to detect IAM policy changes and create findings.
column4: Create a log-based alerting policy from the Logs Explorer with a filter that matches Admin Activity audit log entries containing SetIamPolicy and roles/owner.
column5: Create a user-defined counter metric for SetIamPolicy events and configure an alerting policy with a threshold greater than zero.
column6: Create a SQL-based alerting policy that queries for SetIamPolicy events with roles/owner in the admin activity logs.
column8: Log-based alerting policies scan individual log entries in near real time and send notifications when specific message patterns appear. This approach is ideal for detecting individual security-relevant events like IAM policy changes granting owner access. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/alerting/log-based-alerts

column2: You are writing a YARA-L detection rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) to identify multiple failed login attempts by the same user within a 10-minute window. The rule should generate a detection only when 5 or more failed logins occur. Which YARA-L rule structure correctly implements this detection logic?
column3: Use the outcome section to set a counter variable and reference it in a separate aggregation rule that evaluates the threshold.
column4: Create five separate event variables ($e1 through $e5) and specify all five must exist in the condition section within the time window.
column5: Use a match section with the user variable and 'over 10m', then specify '#e >= 5' in the condition section to count event occurrences.
column6: Use a condition section with 'count($e) >= 5' and specify the 10-minute window using a timestamp comparison in the events section.
column8: YARA-L uses the match section to specify time windows and variables to group by, and the condition section uses the '#' operator to count event occurrences. The syntax '#e >= 5' checks that the event variable $e occurs 5 or more times within the match window. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-2-0-syntax

column2: Your security team suspects lateral movement within your Google Cloud environment. A compromised VM in the production subnet may be attempting to communicate with servers in other subnets that it should not normally access. You need to identify VMs that have established unexpected connections to multiple subnets within the past 24 hours using VPC Flow Logs exported to BigQuery. Which query approach should you use?
column3: Query the VPC Flow Logs table in BigQuery and use GROUP BY on jsonPayload.connection.src_ip to count distinct destination subnets, filtering for internal RFC1918 addresses and aggregating by source VM.
column4: Query the VPC Flow Logs table in BigQuery and filter for jsonPayload.reporter='DEST' to capture all incoming traffic volumes sorted by bytes_sent.
column5: Query the VPC Flow Logs table in BigQuery and use DISTINCT on jsonPayload.connection.dest_ip to find all external IP addresses contacted by any VM in the last 24 hours.
column6: Query the VPC Flow Logs table in BigQuery and use COUNT(*) on all flow records grouped by timestamp to identify traffic spikes during off-peak hours.
column8: To detect lateral movement, you need to identify source IPs communicating with an abnormally high number of destination subnets. Grouping by source IP and counting distinct destination subnets reveals VMs scanning or connecting to multiple network segments, which is a key indicator of lateral movement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs

column2: Your organization is implementing VPC Service Controls. The security team requires that VMs inside the perimeter can only access BigQuery and Cloud Storage APIs, even though additional services like Compute Engine are also protected by the perimeter. How should you configure this requirement?
column3: Configure firewall rules on the VPC network to block API traffic to all services except BigQuery and Cloud Storage.
column4: Enable VPC accessible services for the perimeter and configure the allowed services list to include only BigQuery and Cloud Storage APIs.
column5: Create an egress rule that denies all services except BigQuery and Cloud Storage from within the perimeter.
column6: Remove all services except BigQuery and Cloud Storage from the restricted services list in the perimeter configuration.
column8: The VPC accessible services feature limits which services are accessible from network endpoints inside your perimeter to a specific set of services you define. By enabling this feature and specifying only BigQuery and Cloud Storage, VMs inside the perimeter can only access those APIs even if other services are in the restricted services list. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/manage-service-perimeters

column2: You are optimizing detection rules in Google Security Operations (SecOps) and need to check IP addresses against a maintained list of known malicious infrastructure. The list contains thousands of entries and is updated frequently by your threat intelligence team. What is the recommended approach for implementing this in your YARA-L rules?
column3: Write individual 'or' conditions in the events section for each IP address to provide maximum flexibility for future modifications to the detection logic.
column4: Store the IP addresses in a BigQuery table and use '$e.target.ip in EXTERNAL_QUERY(malicious_ips)' to perform a live lookup during rule evaluation.
column5: Configure the outcome section to calculate a risk score using 'if($e.target.ip = [list of IPs], 100, 0)' to assign scores based on matches.
column6: Create a reference list containing the malicious IP addresses and use the 'in %' operator in the events section to check if '$e.target.ip in %malicious_ip_list'.
column8: Reference lists are designed for grouping items that need to be checked against events. Using the 'in %' operator with a reference list in the events section is the recommended approach for checking values against large, frequently updated lists. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-best-practices

column2: You are implementing a detection solution where Cloud Logging data stored in a log bucket with Log Analytics enabled needs to be enriched with external threat intelligence data from a commercial feed stored in a separate BigQuery dataset. You want analysts to query both datasets using SQL without duplicating log data. What should you do?
column3: Create a linked BigQuery dataset for the log bucket, then use BigQuery SQL to JOIN the log view with the external threat intelligence dataset.
column4: Use federated queries from Log Analytics to access the external threat intelligence BigQuery dataset without creating a linked dataset.
column5: Route logs directly to a BigQuery dataset using a log sink, then JOIN with the threat intelligence dataset.
column6: Export threat intelligence data to the log bucket, then query both datasets using Log Analytics SQL.
column8: Creating a linked BigQuery dataset for a log bucket enables BigQuery to read the log data without data duplication or additional ingestion costs. The linked dataset allows SQL JOINs with any other BigQuery dataset, including the external threat intelligence feed, providing unified query access. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-linked-dataset

column2: Your organization wants to build an automated threat hunting workflow that triggers whenever new high-priority IOCs are published to a centralized threat intelligence feed. The workflow should search historical logs in Google Security Operations (SecOps) for matches against these new IOCs. You need to design a solution that minimizes operational overhead and responds to threat intelligence updates in near real-time. What should you do?
column3: Create a Pub/Sub topic to receive threat intelligence updates, deploy a Cloud Function with an Eventarc trigger subscribed to the topic, and use the function to call the Google SecOps Detection Engine API to initiate retrohunts against the new IOCs.
column4: Create a Compute Engine VM running a continuous polling script that checks for new IOCs and directly writes search queries to the Google SecOps SIEM Search page using browser automation.
column5: Configure Cloud Scheduler to periodically poll the threat intelligence feed every 5 minutes, then use a Cloud Function to compare current and previous IOC lists and manually query logs using BigQuery.
column6: Deploy a Cloud Function with an HTTP trigger that external threat intelligence providers call directly, and store results in Cloud Storage for batch processing overnight.
column8: Pub/Sub provides reliable, asynchronous message delivery for threat intelligence updates, and Eventarc triggers enable near real-time invocation of Cloud Functions. The Detection Engine API supports programmatic retrohunt execution to search historical data for new IOC matches. This event-driven architecture minimizes operational overhead by eliminating polling and manual intervention. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/calling/pubsub and https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reference/detection-engine-api

column2: You need to add a widget to your Cloud Monitoring security dashboard that shows the status of alerting policies monitoring Security Command Center findings. You want analysts to quickly identify if there are any open incidents related to security findings. What should you do?
column3: Create a scorecard widget that displays the count of active SCC findings, using red and green thresholds to indicate normal versus elevated states.
column4: Add a text widget with a link to the Cloud Monitoring Alerting page, so analysts can navigate to view all incident details when needed.
column5: Configure a logs panel widget that filters for SCC finding notifications, allowing analysts to review recent security events in real-time.
column6: Add an Alert Policy widget to the dashboard, selecting the alerting policy that monitors your SCC findings log-based metrics, which displays open incidents and threshold violations.
column8: Alert Policy widgets in Cloud Monitoring dashboards display the monitored metric, threshold, and the number of open incidents. This provides analysts with immediate visibility into whether alerting conditions are being met and if action is required. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/manage-alerts

column2: Your organization's threat intelligence team has identified a set of malicious IP addresses associated with an emerging threat campaign targeting your industry. You need to configure Security Command Center to detect when any of your Google Cloud resources communicate with these IP addresses in near-real time. Which approach should you use?
column3: Configure a Security Health Analytics custom module to scan for connections to the identified IP addresses.
column4: Create a Configurable Bad IP custom module for Event Threat Detection with your organization's list of malicious IP addresses.
column5: Enable the built-in Malware: Bad IP detector and wait for Google to update its threat intelligence with your IP addresses.
column6: Export VPC Flow Logs to BigQuery and create scheduled queries to identify connections to the malicious IP addresses.
column8: The Configurable Bad IP custom module allows you to specify a custom list of suspicious IP addresses. When VPC Flow Logs indicate a connection to any supplied IP address, a finding is generated and written to Security Command Center in near-real time. This directly addresses the requirement to detect communications with known malicious IPs identified by your threat intelligence team. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Premium and has received multiple vulnerability findings. You need to prioritize remediation effectively. According to Google Cloud best practices, which factor should you prioritize first when determining which vulnerabilities to remediate?
column3: Resource type, as compute resources should always be prioritized over storage or network resources regardless of severity.
column4: Finding age, as older vulnerabilities represent greater accumulated risk over time and should be remediated first.
column5: Attack exposure scores, as they indicate which findings expose your designated high-value resources through potential attack paths.
column6: Static severity classifications, as CRITICAL findings should always be addressed before HIGH severity findings.
column8: Google Cloud recommends prioritizing vulnerability and misconfiguration findings by attack exposure scores before prioritizing by severity. Attack exposure scores are dynamic indicators calculated based on specific finding instances, affected resources, and the difficulty an attacker would face reaching your high-value resources. This provides more contextual prioritization than static severity levels alone. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/vulnerabilities-prioritize-remediation

column2: Your threat hunting team needs to identify suspicious service account impersonation in your Google Cloud environment using Cloud Logging. You want to detect when service accounts are being used to make API calls from unusual source IP addresses. Which log field should you examine in your Logs Explorer query?
column3: protoPayload.status.code to identify failed authentication attempts from invalid IP addresses.
column4: protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp to identify the IP address of the caller making the API request.
column5: protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail to identify which service account is being used.
column6: resource.labels.project_id to identify which project the service account belongs to.
column8: The callerIp field in requestMetadata captures the IP address from which the API call originated. By correlating this with the authenticated principal, you can identify when service accounts are being accessed from unexpected locations indicating potential credential compromise or unauthorized impersonation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/understanding-audit-logs

column2: Your organization wants to implement Cloud Monitoring alerting policies to detect security anomalies from custom security metrics that will be written by a third-party security appliance. The security team needs to create the alerting policy before the metrics start flowing to ensure immediate detection when the appliance goes live. The metrics will be written to the custom.googleapis.com namespace. What should you do?
column3: Create a PromQL-based alerting policy using the Cloud Monitoring API with metric existence validation disabled.
column4: Create a log-based alerting policy that monitors Cloud Logging for the first occurrence of the custom metric data.
column5: Create a metric-absence alerting policy that triggers when the expected security metrics are not present.
column6: Create the alerting policy using the Google Cloud console by selecting the expected metric type from the menu-driven interface.
column8: PromQL-based alerting policies support the option to disable metric existence validation, allowing you to create alerting policies for metrics that do not yet exist. This capability is particularly useful for configuring alerting policies using infrastructure-as-code tools like Terraform before the metrics are generated. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/promql/promql-in-alerting

column2: Your team has deployed an automated remediation workflow using Security Command Center notifications and Cloud Functions. The Cloud Function successfully receives findings but fails when attempting to remediate resources in other projects within the organization. What should you do to resolve this issue?
column3: Enable the Security Command Center API in all target projects and grant the SCC service agent cross-project access to invoke the Cloud Function.
column4: Modify the NotificationConfig to include the target project IDs in the filter expression so the function receives project context.
column5: Grant the Cloud Function's runtime service account the necessary IAM roles at the organization or folder level to allow cross-project remediation actions.
column6: Redeploy the Cloud Function in each project where remediation is needed, using project-specific NotificationConfig exports for each deployment.
column8: The runtime service account needs permissions on the target resources it will modify. For cross-project remediation, the service account must have IAM roles granted at a higher level in the resource hierarchy (organization or folder) that includes all target projects. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/securing/function-identity

column2: You are performing proactive threat hunting and need to identify anomalous service account impersonation in your Google Cloud environment. Security Command Center has detected a 'Privilege Escalation: Anomalous Impersonation of Service Account for Admin Activity' finding. You want to investigate this activity further using Cloud Logging. Which audit log field should you examine to identify the delegation chain?
column3: protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerSuppliedUserAgent
column4: protoPayload.authenticationInfo.serviceAccountDelegationInfo
column5: protoPayload.response.bindings.members
column6: protoPayload.authorizationInfo.permission
column8: The serviceAccountDelegationInfo field contains information about the service account delegation chain used in an impersonation request. This field shows the sequence of service accounts involved in the impersonation, which is essential for investigating anomalous impersonation detected by Event Threat Detection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/understanding-audit-logs

column2: Your security team has enabled multiple Google Cloud Threat Intelligence (GCTI) curated detection rule sets in Google Security Operations. After two weeks, you notice that one rule set is generating a high volume of detections on known-safe internal assets. You want to reduce false positives while maintaining detection coverage for genuine threats. What should you do?
column3: Disable the entire rule set and create custom YARA-L rules that replicate the detection logic while adding explicit exclusions for internal assets.
column4: Configure rule exclusions for the affected rule set to exclude events based on UDM fields matching your known-safe internal assets such as specific hostnames or IP addresses.
column5: Switch the rule set from Precise mode to Broad mode to reduce the sensitivity of detections and decrease the volume of alerts on internal assets.
column6: Modify the curated detection rules directly in the Rules Editor to add 'not' conditions that exclude your internal asset IP ranges and hostnames.
column8: Rule exclusions are specifically designed for curated detections to reduce detection volume by defining criteria that prevent certain events from being evaluated. This allows you to exclude known-safe assets while maintaining coverage. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/use-curated-detections

column2: Your organization is approaching the Event Threat Detection custom module quota limit and needs to consolidate custom modules. You have multiple Configurable Bad IP modules, each detecting different threat categories. What is the maximum number of custom modules allowed per organization, and what is a key limitation you should consider when consolidating IP lists into fewer modules?
column3: The default quota is 200 custom modules. Each module has a 6 MB size limit, so consolidated IP lists must fit within this constraint.
column4: The default quota is 500 custom modules. Each module can only contain 1000 IP addresses in the detection parameters.
column5: The default quota is 100 custom modules. Each module can generate a maximum of 100 findings per hour, limiting detection frequency.
column6: The default quota is 200 custom modules. Consolidated modules cannot mix different severity levels, requiring separate modules per threat category.
column8: Event Threat Detection custom modules have a default quota of 200 modules per organization and each module has a maximum size of 6 MB. When consolidating multiple IP lists into fewer modules, you must ensure the combined JSON configuration including all IP addresses, metadata, severity, and recommendations does not exceed this 6 MB limit. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Threat hunting"Your organization recently enabled Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) in Google Security Operations (SecOps). You want to understand how IOC matches are prioritized to focus your threat hunting efforts on the most critical indicators. Which statement accurately describes how ATI prioritizes IOCs?
column3: ATI requires manual priority assignment by analysts for each IOC match before generating alerts for the detection dashboard.
column4: ATI uses the Google Threat Intelligence (GTI) score to prioritize IOCs, assigning labels like Active Breach, High, and Medium based on confidence and threat severity.
column5: ATI prioritizes IOCs based solely on the number of assets affected, with higher asset counts receiving Active Breach priority classification.
column6: ATI assigns priority based on chronological order, with the most recently discovered IOCs receiving the highest priority level.
column8: Google SecOps now uses the Google Threat Intelligence (GTI) score for prioritization in Applied Threat Intelligence. The GTI score delivers a unified verdict aggregating threat intelligence data and assigns priority labels such as Active Breach, High, or Medium to IOCs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-curated-detections

column2: Your organization is using Security Command Center Enterprise with ticketing system integration. You want to ensure that when all findings in a case are addressed, the case is automatically closed without manual intervention. An analyst has muted all the findings in a case because they were determined to be acceptable risk. What happens to the case after all findings are muted?
column3: The case priority is automatically lowered to informational, but the case stays open for tracking.
column4: The case remains open but is moved to a separate 'Muted Cases' queue for periodic review.
column5: Security Command Center automatically closes the case when all findings in it are muted.
column6: The case remains unchanged and must be manually closed by an analyst after verification.
column8: When you mute all findings in a case, Security Command Center Enterprise automatically closes the case. This prevents muted findings from continuing to consume analyst attention and ensures the case queue reflects only active, unmuted findings that require triage. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/mute-findings-in-cases

column2: Your security operations team has configured an SLO for a critical authentication service with a 99.5% availability target over a 30-day rolling compliance period. The team wants to receive alerts that warn them well before the error budget is fully depleted, while avoiding excessive alert noise from short-lived issues. Which alerting configuration should you implement?
column3: Create a burn-rate alerting policy with a threshold of 0.03% hourly consumption and a 1-minute lookback duration.
column4: Configure an alerting policy that triggers when the remaining error budget drops below 50% of the total budget allocated for the compliance period.
column5: Configure a burn-rate alerting policy with a slow-burn threshold of 2x the baseline consumption rate and a 24-hour lookback duration.
column6: Configure an alerting policy on the availability metric with a threshold of 0.5% error rate and a 5-minute evaluation window.
column8: A burn-rate alerting policy monitors how quickly your error budget is being consumed. A slow-burn alert with a 2x baseline threshold and 24-hour lookback period is a recommended starting point that detects sustained issues that would eventually deplete the error budget while avoiding alerts from brief spikes. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/alerting-on-budget-burn-rate

column2: A security incident has been detected, and you must immediately place a legal hold on specific Cloud Storage objects that contain forensic artifacts while an investigation is ongoing. The retention duration is unknown at this time. Which Cloud Storage feature should you use?
column3: Configure a bucket-level retention policy without locking it, setting a long retention period that can be extended if needed.
column4: Enable Object Retention Lock on the bucket and set retain-until times on specific objects in locked mode.
column5: Apply temporary holds to the specific objects containing forensic artifacts to prevent deletion until the hold is explicitly released.
column6: Apply event-based holds to the objects and configure the bucket with a suitable retention policy that triggers when the hold is released.
column8: Temporary holds prevent objects from being deleted or replaced regardless of any retention policy, and they have no expiration date. This makes them ideal for legal holds where the retention duration is unknown. The hold remains until explicitly released by an authorized user. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/object-holds

column2: You have created an Event Threat Detection custom module at the organization level to detect connections to malicious IP addresses. A project team within your organization needs to disable this detection for their specific project while keeping it enabled for all other projects. How should you accomplish this?
column3: Delete the organization-level custom module and recreate it individually in each project where detection is needed.
column4: Disable the inherited custom module at the project level, which only affects that specific project without changing the organization-level configuration.
column5: Create an exclusion rule in the organization-level custom module to exempt the specific project's resources from detection.
column6: Modify the organization-level custom module to add a project filter that excludes the specific project from scanning.
column8: When you disable an inherited custom module at the project level, the changes are only applied to that project. The original custom module residing at the parent organization level is not affected, and other projects continue to inherit the enabled module. This provides granular control over detection settings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: A security analyst on your team wants to reduce noise from irrelevant Security Health Analytics findings that are constantly appearing in cases. The analyst mutes all findings within a specific case. What happens to the case after all findings are muted?
column3: The case is archived for 30 days before being permanently deleted, allowing for potential unmuting of findings.
column4: Security Command Center automatically closes the case because all findings within it are muted.
column5: The case remains open and the muted findings are hidden from view but continue to affect case priority.
column6: The case remains open but is moved to a low-priority queue for future review by analysts.
column8: When you mute all findings in a case, Security Command Center automatically closes the case. Muting findings prevents them from appearing in cases, and when no active or unmuted findings remain, the case lifecycle ends. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/mute-findings-in-cases

column2: Your organization uses Event Threat Detection in Security Command Center Premium at the organization level. The security team wants to detect malware by monitoring DNS queries across your environment. You want to enable the required logging with cost optimization in mind. Which log source should you enable?
column3: VPC Flow Logs with the default aggregation interval and 50% sample rate for comprehensive network visibility.
column4: Cloud DNS logging, which provides sufficient visibility for Event Threat Detection to detect malware using domain resolution.
column5: Data Access audit logs enabled for all services to capture comprehensive access patterns for malware detection.
column6: Admin Activity audit logs, which are automatically written and provide malware detection capabilities.
column8: Cloud DNS logging provides sufficient visibility for Event Threat Detection to detect malware using domain resolution. For most users, Cloud DNS logs are sufficient for the network detection of malware, and this is the most cost-effective option compared to VPC Flow Logs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your organization runs workloads on Amazon Web Services (AWS) that need to access data stored in Google Cloud Storage. You want to configure authentication that follows least privilege principles and eliminates the need for long-lived credentials. What should you do?
column3: Configure Workload Identity Federation with an AWS identity provider, create a dedicated service account with only the required Cloud Storage permissions, and grant the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser role to specific AWS principals.
column4: Create a service account key for a service account with Storage Object Admin permissions, store the key in AWS Secrets Manager, and configure the AWS workload to use Application Default Credentials with the key.
column5: Configure Workload Identity Federation and grant the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser role to all members of the workload identity pool on a service account with Storage Admin permissions at the project level.
column6: Create a Compute Engine default service account with Editor permissions and share the service account credentials with the AWS workload through a secure channel.
column8: Workload Identity Federation allows AWS workloads to authenticate using their native AWS credentials without service account keys. Creating a dedicated service account with minimal permissions follows least privilege, and granting workloadIdentityUser to specific principals rather than all pool members prevents over-permissioning. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation

column2: Observability"Your security team requires the roles/securitycenter.notificationConfigEditor IAM role to manage notification configurations for Security Command Center findings. A team member with this role reports they cannot create a new NotificationConfig. What additional permission or role is most likely missing?
column3: The Security Center Admin role (roles/securitycenter.admin) at the organization level.
column4: The securitycenter.notification.create permission added via a custom role at the folder level.
column5: The Project IAM Admin role (roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin) on the SCC project.
column6: The Pub/Sub Admin role (roles/pubsub.admin) on the target Pub/Sub topic.
column8: Creating a NotificationConfig requires both SCC notification permissions and Pub/Sub Admin role on the topic that will receive notifications. When the NotificationConfig is created, SCC automatically grants the securitycenter.notificationServiceAgent role to its service account on the topic, which requires pubsub.topics.setIamPolicy permission. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-notifications

column2: Your organization uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) to establish user activity baselines and detect anomalies. You need to understand how entity risk scores are calculated and normalized to properly interpret the Risk Analytics dashboard. Which statement accurately describes the entity risk score calculation in Google SecOps?
column3: Entity risk scores are calculated in real-time using machine learning algorithms that compare current behavior against peer group baselines with scores ranging from 0-100.
column4: Entity risk scores are calculated using prevalence statistics that measure how commonly an entity's activity patterns occur across the enterprise environment.
column5: Entity risk scores are static values assigned by detection rules and do not change based on the selected risk calculation window.
column6: Base entity risk scores are calculated by adding risk scores across findings for an entity during the risk window with weighting applied, then normalized to a range of 1-1000.
column8: Google SecOps calculates entity risk scores by aggregating the risk scores from findings (alerts and detections) within the selected risk window. Weighting defines how alert and detection risk scores contribute to the calculation, and scores are normalized using min-max normalization to a range of 1-1000, with entities having a 0 risk score excluded from the dashboard. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/risk-analytics-overview

column2: Your incident response team is investigating a potential data exfiltration event. You need to aggregate logs from multiple Google Cloud projects across your organization into a centralized location for forensic analysis. The logs must be searchable using SQL queries while maintaining a complete audit trail. What is the most effective approach?
column3: Export logs from each project using the gcloud logging read command to local storage, consolidate them manually, and import into a SIEM for centralized analysis.
column4: Create a Pub/Sub topic in each project, configure log sinks to publish to the topics, then use Dataflow to merge the streams into a single BigQuery table for analysis.
column5: Create an aggregated sink at the organization level that routes logs to a centralized log bucket, upgrade the bucket to use Log Analytics, and create a linked BigQuery dataset for SQL-based forensic queries.
column6: Configure individual log sinks in each project to export logs to a shared Cloud Storage bucket, then use BigQuery external tables to query the JSON log files for analysis.
column8: Aggregated sinks at the organization or folder level can route logs from multiple projects to a centralized destination. Upgrading the log bucket to Log Analytics enables SQL queries directly on log data, and linking to BigQuery provides additional analytical capabilities for forensic investigation. This maintains logs in their native format while enabling powerful analysis. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview

column2: Your security team is implementing log-based detection in Google Cloud and needs to analyze Admin Activity audit logs to identify potential privilege escalation attempts, such as IAM policy changes granting sensitive roles. The team requires the ability to aggregate findings, identify patterns across multiple log entries, and create visualizations. Which tool should you recommend for this analysis?
column3: Use Log Analytics with SQL queries to analyze the Admin Activity audit logs stored in a Log Analytics-upgraded bucket.
column4: Create log-based metrics for each IAM change type and view the metrics individually in Cloud Monitoring dashboards.
column5: Use Logs Explorer with advanced filters to search Admin Activity audit logs and manually review matching entries.
column6: Configure a log sink to export Admin Activity logs to Cloud Storage and use gsutil commands to analyze the exported files.
column8: Log Analytics supports SQL queries that can aggregate data, identify patterns across multiple log entries, and create visualizations. It is specifically recommended for generating insights and trends from logs, including security analysis use cases like detecting privilege escalation through IAM changes. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-and-view

column2: Your organization requires security logs exported to BigQuery to be retained for exactly 90 days before automatic deletion. You are configuring a new Cloud Logging sink to a BigQuery dataset and want to implement cost-effective storage management. What should you configure?
column3: Configure the sink to use partitioned tables and set the table expiration to 90 days in the BigQuery dataset settings.
column4: Configure the sink to use partitioned tables and set a partition expiration of 90 days at the dataset level or on the individual tables.
column5: Configure the sink to use a linked BigQuery dataset from a Log Analytics-upgraded bucket with 90-day retention.
column6: Configure the sink to use date-sharded tables and create a Cloud Function to delete tables older than 90 days on a daily schedule.
column8: Partitioned tables support partition expiration settings that automatically delete data older than the specified duration. Setting partition expiration at the dataset level applies the default to all tables, while table-level settings can override this. This provides automated lifecycle management for compliance and cost control. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/managing-partitioned-tables

column2: Web Security Scanner has detected an XSS_CALLBACK finding in your production application. The security operations team needs to validate the finding before escalating to development. According to Google Cloud best practices, what is the recommended approach to reproduce and validate this vulnerability?
column3: Configure a second Web Security Scanner scan targeting only the affected URL to confirm the vulnerability exists.
column4: Review Cloud Audit Logs for the Web Security Scanner service account activities during the scan timeframe.
column5: Follow the Reproduction URL link provided in the finding details in the Google Cloud console to verify if the attack can execute code.
column6: Export the finding JSON definition to BigQuery and analyze the payload patterns used during detection.
column8: Web Security Scanner provides a Reproduction URL that directly opens an alert dialog or injects the string XSSDETECTED to prove the attack can execute code. This allows security teams to validate findings before escalation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-remediate-web-security-scanner-findings

column2: You are configuring threat detection for your production GKE clusters and want to enable runtime threat detection to identify active threats such as cryptomining, privilege escalation, and malicious code execution. You have Security Command Center Premium activated. What must you verify before Container Threat Detection can function on your clusters?
column3: Verify that all clusters have Binary Authorization enabled in enforcing mode to allow Container Threat Detection to verify container image signatures during runtime monitoring.
column4: Verify that Cloud IDS is enabled for the VPC network to allow Container Threat Detection to correlate network-based indicators with container runtime events.
column5: Verify that all nodes are running Ubuntu-based images, as Container Threat Detection only supports Ubuntu node images for runtime threat monitoring and detection.
column6: Verify that GKE Sandbox is disabled on clusters where you want Container Threat Detection deployed, as the two features are incompatible with each other.
column8: Container Threat Detection is not compatible with GKE Sandbox. GKE Sandbox provides an additional layer of isolation using gVisor, which prevents Container Threat Detection from accessing the low-level kernel events it needs for detection. This feature must be disabled on clusters where you want Container Threat Detection deployed. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-container-threat-detection

column2: You are creating a sensitive data classification baseline for your organization's security operations. You need to detect organization-specific identifiers such as employee IDs and internal project codes that follow a specific pattern alongside standard PII. Which approach should you use with Cloud DLP?
column3: Configure hotword rules on the built-in PERSON_NAME infoType to increase likelihood when employee ID patterns appear nearby.
column4: Create a stored infoType in BigQuery containing all existing employee IDs and project codes, and reference it in every inspection request.
column5: Use only built-in infoTypes like GENERIC_ID and adjust the likelihood threshold to capture organization-specific patterns automatically.
column6: Create an inspection template with both built-in infoTypes for standard PII and custom infoType detectors using regex patterns for your organization-specific identifiers.
column8: Inspection templates provide a reusable configuration that can include both built-in infoTypes and custom infoType detectors. Custom regex detectors allow you to define patterns that match organization-specific identifiers, ensuring consistent classification across all scanning operations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/creating-templates-inspect

column2: Your security team is using Security Command Center Enterprise and notices that many low-severity Security Health Analytics findings are cluttering their case queue, preventing analysts from focusing on critical issues. You need to implement a solution that automatically prevents these low-severity findings from appearing in cases while ensuring they are still logged for compliance purposes. What should you do?
column3: Configure dynamic mute rules to mute low-severity findings, which prevents them from appearing in cases while maintaining audit logs.
column4: Configure the SCC Enterprise connector to filter out low-severity findings during ingestion.
column5: Disable the Security Health Analytics detectors that generate low-severity findings to stop case creation entirely.
column6: Delete the low-severity cases manually from the case queue as they appear to keep the queue manageable.
column8: Dynamic mute rules automatically mute current and future findings that match specified criteria. When findings are muted, they are hidden from cases and the default view but continue to be logged for audit and compliance purposes. Dynamic mute rules are the recommended approach for controlling finding volume. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-mute-findings

column2: Your organization wants to continuously monitor running GKE workloads for container images that violate security policies after initial deployment, including images deployed via breakglass during incident response. What should you configure?
column3: Configure Binary Authorization enforcement mode to ENFORCED_BLOCK_AND_AUDIT_LOG on all clusters to monitor running workloads.
column4: Enable Binary Authorization continuous validation (CV) with check-based platform policies and configure checks for trusted directories, image freshness, and vulnerabilities.
column5: Configure Security Command Center Container Threat Detection to monitor for policy violations in running containers.
column6: Enable Artifact Analysis automatic scanning on all Artifact Registry repositories and configure Pub/Sub notifications for new vulnerabilities.
column8: CV with check-based platform policies periodically monitors Pods running on GKE to ensure their associated container images continue to conform to specified policies. Unlike enforcement which only validates at deploy time, CV continues to regularly log policy-violating Pods, including those deployed using breakglass. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/overview-cv

column2: Your threat hunting team needs to detect when external users are added to highly-privileged Google Groups that have sensitive IAM roles assigned. This activity could indicate privilege escalation. You need to configure the appropriate log sources and query approach. What should you do?
column3: Create a SQL query in Log Analytics that joins Admin Activity logs with Google Workspace logs using the group email as the correlation key.
column4: Monitor only SetIamPolicy calls in Admin Activity logs since they contain the complete list of group members receiving new permissions.
column5: Enable Google Workspace log sharing with Google Cloud, query Admin Activity audit logs for IAM role grants to groups, and correlate with Google Workspace logs for group membership changes.
column6: Query Data Access audit logs for GetIamPolicy calls and examine the response field to identify all groups with privileged roles and their current members.
column8: Cloud Audit Logs record IAM role grants to groups but do not contain information on individual group members. By sharing Google Workspace logs with Google Cloud, you can correlate group membership changes with the sensitive roles assigned to those groups to detect privilege escalation through group manipulation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your security team needs to provide administrators with SSH access to Linux VMs that do not have public IP addresses. You want to implement a context-aware access solution that eliminates the need for bastion hosts or VPN connections while still enforcing identity-based access controls. What should you do?
column3: Configure a Cloud NAT gateway for the subnet containing the VMs and grant administrators the Compute Instance Admin role, then use standard SSH clients to connect through the NAT.
column4: Enable Private Google Access on the subnet and configure IAP to forward SSH traffic through the private.googleapis.com endpoint, then assign the Compute OS Login role to administrators.
column5: Enable IAP TCP forwarding and grant administrators the IAP-Secured Tunnel User role on the target VMs, then configure firewall rules to allow ingress from the IAP IP range 35.235.240.0/20 on port 22.
column6: Deploy an IAP connector in the VPC network and configure the VMs to register with the connector, then grant administrators access through the IAP connector's web interface.
column8: IAP TCP forwarding allows SSH access to VMs without public IP addresses by tunneling traffic through IAP. Users need the IAP-Secured Tunnel User role to create tunnels, and firewall rules must allow traffic from IAP's IP range (35.235.240.0/20) to reach the SSH port. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/using-tcp-forwarding

column2: Platform operations"You are configuring a Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR playbook for automated malware response. The playbook needs to enrich file hash entities using VirusTotal, make decisions based on the enrichment results, and quarantine files if they are malicious. Sensitive actions like quarantine should require human approval before execution. How should you configure the playbook actions?
column3: Configure both actions as Automatic with Time to respond deadlines, and use the If previous action fails flow to skip quarantine if the deadline expires.
column4: Configure all actions as Automatic and use the Expression Builder to prevent quarantine execution when VirusTotal returns non-malicious results.
column5: Configure the VirusTotal enrichment action as Automatic, add a Condition flow based on the enrichment JSON result, and set the quarantine action to Manual with assignment to a SOC role.
column6: Configure the VirusTotal action as Manual for accuracy verification, add a Multi-Choice Question flow for the analyst, and set quarantine to Automatic for fast response.
column8: Playbook actions can be configured as Automatic or Manual. Enrichment actions that gather data should run automatically. The Condition flow allows branching based on previous action results (like VirusTotal scores). Sensitive actions like quarantine should be set to Manual and assigned to a user or SOC role, which pauses the playbook until human approval. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/using-actions-in-playbooks

column2: You have enabled Event Threat Detection for your Google Cloud organization but notice that some threat categories are not generating findings. You want to maximize the threat detection capabilities of Event Threat Detection. Which logs should you review to ensure they are enabled?
column3: Only Admin Activity audit logs need to be enabled because Event Threat Detection primarily relies on these logs for all threat detection capabilities.
column4: Google Workspace logs must be enabled at the project level because Event Threat Detection requires these logs for detecting identity-based threats.
column5: All logs are enabled automatically when Event Threat Detection is activated, and no additional log configuration is required to maximize detection coverage.
column6: Data access audit logs, Cloud DNS logs, and VPC Flow Logs should be reviewed because some of these logs that Event Threat Detection scans are disabled by default and must be explicitly enabled.
column8: Event Threat Detection scans specific logs to detect threats, and some logs like data access audit logs and VPC Flow Logs are turned off by default. Admin Activity audit logs are always on and scanned automatically, but other log types require explicit enablement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your incident response team suspects lateral movement within your GKE cluster after detecting suspicious activity on a compromised Pod. You need to analyze VPC Flow Logs to trace the network connections made by Pods within the cluster. You have enabled intranode visibility for the GKE cluster. What information should you use from VPC Flow Logs to correlate network flows with specific Pods?
column3: Use the GKE metadata annotations in VPC Flow Logs that include Pod name, namespace, and cluster information to map flows to specific workloads.
column4: Use the source and destination VM instance names from VPC Flow Logs to identify which GKE nodes hosted the communicating Pods.
column5: Export VPC Flow Logs to BigQuery and join with Kubernetes API audit logs using timestamp correlation to determine which Pods were active during each flow.
column6: Query the source and destination port numbers from VPC Flow Logs and match them against known service ports in your GKE Services configuration.
column8: When intranode visibility is enabled for GKE, VPC Flow Logs include GKE metadata annotations that contain details about the source and destination endpoints including Pod name, namespace, and cluster information. These annotations enable correlation of network flows with specific Kubernetes workloads for lateral movement analysis. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/about-flow-logs-records

column2: Your security team needs to create an automated threat hunting pipeline where SCC Event Threat Detection findings trigger a Cloud Function via Pub/Sub to search for related IOCs in historical logs. You must configure SCC to publish findings to the Pub/Sub topic. Which component should you configure to enable this integration?
column3: Create a SCC notification configuration with a filter for Event Threat Detection findings that publishes to the Pub/Sub topic.
column4: Configure an Eventarc trigger on the Cloud Function to directly receive SCC findings without using Pub/Sub.
column5: Enable SCC streaming export directly to the Cloud Function endpoint URL.
column6: Create a Cloud Logging sink with a filter for SCC findings that routes to a Cloud Function trigger.
column8: Security Command Center notifications enable findings to be sent to a Pub/Sub topic based on filter criteria. You can filter by source, category, or severity to target specific finding types like Event Threat Detection findings for automated threat hunting workflows. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-notifications

column2: Your detection engineering team has identified that Web Security Scanner managed scans are detecting XSS and SQL injection vulnerabilities in your production applications. However, you need to scan authenticated areas of your web applications that require user login. What should you do to improve detection coverage?
column3: Configure Web Security Scanner custom scans with Google Account authentication or custom authentication credentials for the applications requiring authenticated scanning.
column4: Enable Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy for your applications and configure managed scans to pass through IAP authentication automatically.
column5: Create service accounts with appropriate IAM roles and configure managed scans to use service account impersonation for authenticated scanning.
column6: Modify the managed scan settings to include authentication credentials for each application endpoint.
column8: Custom scans support authentication methods including Google Account authentication, allowing the scanner to access authenticated areas of web applications. Managed scans send GET-only requests and don't use authentication, so custom scans are required for authenticated scanning. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-web-security-scanner-custom-scans

column2: You are analyzing Cloud Asset Inventory data exported to BigQuery to identify all Compute Engine instances across your organization. When writing SQL queries against the exported data, how should you reference the Compute Engine instance asset type in the table name?
column3: compute_googleapis_com_Instance
column4: compute.googleapis.com/Instance
column5: ComputeInstance
column6: google.compute.Instance
column8: When Cloud Asset Inventory exports data to BigQuery, asset type names have periods and slashes replaced with underscores. The asset type compute.googleapis.com/Instance becomes compute_googleapis_com_Instance as the BigQuery table name. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/query-assets

column2: You are configuring Container Threat Detection for a production GKE cluster that runs a CI/CD system with significant file I/O operations. The security team wants to enable file monitoring detectors to detect access or modification to critical system files. You need to ensure the detectors are enabled while minimizing performance impact on workloads. What should you do?
column3: Evaluate the performance impact of file monitoring detectors on a non-production workload before enabling them in production since these detectors are disabled by default.
column4: Enable all Container Threat Detection modules immediately since file monitoring detectors have minimal performance impact on modern GKE clusters.
column5: Deploy a separate dedicated GKE cluster specifically for file monitoring detection to isolate the performance impact from your CI/CD workloads.
column6: Configure Cloud Monitoring alerts to track file operations instead of enabling Container Threat Detection file monitoring since it provides lower overhead.
column8: Container Threat Detection file monitoring detectors are disabled by default due to potential performance degradation on workloads with significant file I/O like CI/CD systems. Google recommends evaluating the impact on any workload before enabling these detectors in production environments. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: You are configuring Cloud Logging for security analysis and need to enable analysts to join log data with external threat intelligence datasets stored in BigQuery. The analysts should be able to compare URLs found in logs against a BigQuery table containing known malicious URLs. What configuration should you implement?
column3: Use Log Analytics SQL queries with the EXTERNAL_QUERY function to access the threat intelligence dataset during analysis.
column4: Upgrade the log bucket to use Log Analytics and create a linked BigQuery dataset to enable cross-dataset queries.
column5: Configure a log sink to export logs directly to BigQuery and manually configure table partitioning for the exported logs.
column6: Create a scheduled Dataflow pipeline to extract URLs from logs and match them against the threat intelligence dataset.
column8: Creating a linked BigQuery dataset on a Log Analytics-upgraded bucket allows BigQuery to read log data and enables joining log data with other BigQuery datasets, such as external threat intelligence data containing malicious URLs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-linked-dataset

column2: Your security team needs a Cloud Monitoring dashboard that displays Security Command Center vulnerability findings grouped by resource type. The dashboard should show a table widget listing the top 10 resource types with the most active findings. How should you configure this?
column3: Export SCC findings to Cloud Storage in JSON format, create a scheduled Cloud Function to aggregate findings by resource type, and write the results as custom metrics.
column4: Create a user-defined log-based metric with resource_type as a label extracted from SCC finding logs, then add a TimeSeriesTable widget to your dashboard with appropriate grouping and sorting.
column5: Configure a scorecard widget in the Cloud Monitoring dashboard that queries the securitycenter.googleapis.com/findings metric directly from the SCC API.
column6: Use Monitoring Query Language (MQL) to directly query Security Command Center findings by resource type and display results in a table widget.
column8: User-defined log-based metrics can include labels extracted from log entry fields, such as resource_type. The TimeSeriesTable widget in Cloud Monitoring can display this data grouped by the label and sorted to show top values. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics

column2: Your organization has experienced a security incident and you need to preserve Cloud Audit Logs for forensic investigation. The legal team requires that the logs be retained for 7 years to meet regulatory compliance requirements. The logs are currently stored in the _Default log bucket with the default 30-day retention. What should you do to meet the legal team's requirements?
column3: Extend the retention period of the _Default log bucket to 2555 days and enable CMEK encryption on the bucket to protect the evidence.
column4: Configure a log sink to export all audit logs to BigQuery with a dataset retention policy of 7 years, then use scheduled queries to archive the data monthly.
column5: Modify the _Required log bucket retention period to 2555 days since Cloud Audit Logs are automatically stored there with compliance-grade protection.
column6: Create a user-defined log bucket with a custom retention period of 2555 days, configure a log sink to route audit logs to the new bucket, and apply a CMEK for additional encryption protection.
column8: Cloud Logging allows you to configure retention periods between 1 day and 3650 days on user-defined log buckets. Creating a dedicated bucket for forensic logs with a 7-year (2555 days) retention period ensures compliance. Using CMEK provides an additional layer of encryption control for sensitive evidence. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets

column2: You are deploying VPC Service Controls in a production environment that contains critical workloads. Before enforcing the perimeter, you want to identify which legitimate requests would be blocked without disrupting current operations. What should you do?
column3: Create the service perimeter in enforced mode with broad access levels, then gradually restrict access levels based on observed traffic patterns.
column4: Create the service perimeter in dry run mode, monitor the policy violation logs in Cloud Logging, and progressively refine the configuration before switching to enforced mode.
column5: Apply the service perimeter to only non-critical projects first, monitor for any issues, then expand to critical projects after validation.
column6: Create duplicate projects in a test environment, apply the perimeter in enforced mode to the test projects, and replicate the configuration to production after testing.
column8: Dry run mode logs violations as though the perimeters are enforced but does not prevent access to restricted services. This allows you to understand the effect of enabling VPC Service Controls and identify any issues before enforcement. Using dry run mode before switching to enforced mode is recommended as a best practice. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode

column2: You are configuring Cloud Monitoring to track SLO compliance for your organization's incident response API. The security team needs to create a dashboard that displays real-time SLO performance data and wants to understand the different time-series selectors available. Which time-series selector should you use to display the current ratio of good requests to total requests during a specific alignment period?
column3: Use the select_slo_health time-series selector to retrieve the ratio of good requests to total requests during the alignment period.
column4: Use the select_slo_counts time-series selector to display the absolute number of good and bad requests during the alignment period.
column5: Use the select_slo_burn_rate time-series selector to calculate how quickly the error budget is being consumed relative to the sustainable failure rate.
column6: Use the select_slo_compliance time-series selector to retrieve the ratio of good units to total units since the start of the compliance period.
column8: The select_slo_health time-series selector answers the question 'During a given alignment period, what was the ratio of good requests to total requests?' This provides real-time visibility into service performance where a value of 1 indicates all requests were good. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/api/timeseries-selectors

column2: Your security team wants to detect and alert on a high-severity pattern where an unusually large number of failed authentication attempts occur against service accounts within a 10-minute window. You need to configure an alerting mechanism that counts these events and triggers when they exceed a threshold. Which approach should you use?
column3: Create a counter-type log-based metric with a filter matching authentication failure events, then configure a metric-based alerting policy with a threshold condition.
column4: Create a log-based alerting policy that triggers on each individual authentication failure event and set the minimum time between notifications to 10 minutes.
column5: Configure a log sink to export authentication logs to BigQuery and create a scheduled query that alerts when failures exceed the threshold.
column6: Create a distribution-type log-based metric to aggregate the authentication failures and configure an alerting policy based on the mean value.
column8: Counter-type log-based metrics are designed to count log entries matching a filter. Combined with a metric-based alerting policy, you can set thresholds to detect when the count exceeds acceptable levels within a rolling window, which is ideal for detecting patterns of repeated security events. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/counter-metrics

column2: Your security team requires security-related logs from all projects in your organization to be exported to a centralized BigQuery dataset for threat analysis. The logs must be available for querying with optimal performance and cost efficiency. You need to configure log routing to meet these requirements. What should you do?
column3: Create project-level sinks with partitioned tables in each project and use BigQuery federated queries to join the distributed datasets.
column4: Create project-level sinks in each project with date-sharded tables enabled and route logs to separate BigQuery datasets in each project.
column5: Create an organization-level aggregated sink with partitioned tables enabled and route logs to a centralized BigQuery dataset in a dedicated security project.
column6: Create an organization-level aggregated sink and route logs to a linked BigQuery dataset created from a Log Analytics-enabled log bucket.
column8: Aggregated sinks at the organization level collect logs from all child projects and route them to a single destination. Partitioned tables provide better query performance and cost efficiency compared to date-sharded tables by maintaining a single schema and metadata set. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks and https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery

column2: Threat hunting"Your organization uses Log Analytics in Cloud Logging to run SQL queries for threat hunting. You need to join your Cloud Logging data with external threat intelligence feeds stored in a separate BigQuery dataset. What should you do to enable this analysis?
column3: Export logs from Cloud Logging to Cloud Storage in JSON format, then load both the logs and threat intelligence data into BigQuery for querying.
column4: Upgrade the log bucket to use Log Analytics, and create a linked BigQuery dataset for the log bucket to enable BigQuery to query the log data and join it with other datasets.
column5: Configure a log sink to route logs directly to the linked BigQuery dataset containing your threat intelligence data for automatic correlation.
column6: Create a separate Cloud Logging log bucket for the threat intelligence data and use Log Analytics to join the two log buckets together.
column8: Creating a linked BigQuery dataset allows you to query log data stored in Cloud Logging buckets using BigQuery SQL, which enables JOINs with other BigQuery datasets including threat intelligence feeds. This approach maintains log storage in Cloud Logging while enabling advanced analytics. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-linked-dataset

column2: You are configuring Event Threat Detection in Security Command Center for an organization. After enabling the service, your team notices that certain threat categories are not generating findings even though suspicious activities are occurring. You want to ensure all relevant detectors are working. What should you verify?
column3: Verify that the Event Threat Detection API is enabled in each project where you want threat detection, as the service must be activated individually at the project level.
column4: Verify that custom modules have been created for each threat category, as Event Threat Detection only uses custom modules and has no built-in detection capabilities.
column5: Verify that the required Cloud Logging logs are enabled, as some logs that Event Threat Detection scans are turned off by default and must be explicitly enabled before detectors can generate findings.
column6: Verify that Google Threat Intelligence has been connected through the Security Command Center integration settings to enable threat feeds for detection modules.
column8: Event Threat Detection generates findings by scanning specific logs, and some of these logs are turned off by default. For example, Data Access audit logs for many services are disabled by default. You must enable the relevant logs before Event Threat Detection can scan them and generate findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-event-threat-detection

column2: You are building a Looker Studio dashboard to track security operations KPIs using Security Command Center findings exported to BigQuery. The security team needs to visualize the mean time to remediate (MTTR) for critical findings. The BigQuery table contains event_time and state_change_time columns that track when findings are created and when their state changes to INACTIVE. You need to create a metric that calculates the average remediation time. What should you do?
column3: Use the comparison metric feature in Looker Studio to compare event_time against state_change_time and display the percentage difference.
column4: Export the findings data from Looker Studio to Google Sheets, calculate MTTR using spreadsheet formulas, then reimport the results as a new data source.
column5: Create a calculated field in the Looker Studio data source using a formula that calculates the date difference between state_change_time and event_time, then aggregate using the AVG function.
column6: Write a SQL query in BigQuery that pre-calculates MTTR as a new column, then connect Looker Studio to the modified table without using calculated fields.
column8: Calculated fields in Looker Studio let you create new metrics derived from your data. Using date functions to compute the time difference between finding creation and remediation, then averaging the results, provides an accurate MTTR calculation. Creating this at the data source level allows reuse across multiple charts. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio/about-calculated-fields

column2: Your security operations team wants to create a custom metric in Cloud Monitoring to track the number of failed authentication attempts across your application. The metric will be used in alerting policies to detect potential brute-force attacks. Which metric type prefix should you use when creating this user-defined metric?
column3: security.googleapis.com/
column4: monitoring.googleapis.com/
column5: compute.googleapis.com/
column6: custom.googleapis.com/
column8: Custom.googleapis.com/ is one of the allowable prefixes for user-defined metrics in Cloud Monitoring. When you create a user-defined metric, you define a string identifier that represents the metric type, and this string must use a prefix that marks it as a user-defined metric. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/custom-metrics

column2: You are setting up centralized log storage for incident response purposes across your Google Cloud organization. You need to configure Cloud Logging to retain audit logs for 2 years in a central project while ensuring that log deletion is prevented until the retention period expires. Which combination of actions should you take?
column3: Configure the _Required log bucket in the central project with a 730-day retention and add a project lien.
column4: Create a Cloud Storage sink at the organization level and enable Object Versioning with lifecycle rules to retain all versions for 2 years.
column5: Create an organization-level aggregated sink routing to a user-defined log bucket with a 730-day retention period, then lock the log bucket.
